turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (NURSE): Morning, Mrs Hale. I've done your observations. Blood pressure is one hundred and thirty-eight over eighty-two, pulse seventy-eight, temperature thirty-six point seven, oxygen saturations ninety-seven percent, and your breathing rate is sixteen. Doctor will see you now.
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Oh thank you, love. That cuff always makes my arm go tingly. Same as the one in Boots, honestly, I thought it was going to take my hand off last winter.
[SEG0003] person_3 (DOCTOR): Come in, Mrs Hale. I'm Dr Shah. Your sister can stay. What brings you in today?
[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): This cough. It started after the flu and it's been six weeks now. I'm absolutely fed up with it.
[SEG0005] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): She is. I'm Linda, her sister. We're both losing sleep over it.
[SEG0006] person_3 (DOCTOR): Six weeks, after the flu. When is the cough at its worst?
[SEG0007] person_2 (PATIENT): Nights, definitely. I'm hacking away at two in the morning. The dog thinks it's time for a walk, daft thing.
[SEG0008] person_3 (DOCTOR): Any phlegm with the cough?
[SEG0009] person_2 (PATIENT): He's a rescue terrier from Margate, my husband's idea before he passed. He still barks at the postman every single day.
[SEG0010] person_3 (DOCTOR): He sounds lively. Just coming back to what I asked — is there phlegm when you cough?
[SEG0011] person_2 (PATIENT): Sorry, doctor, I do wander. Um, not really, it's a dry cough. Well, actually, a tiny bit of clear stuff first thing, nothing green or horrible.
[SEG0012] person_3 (DOCTOR): Any blood in the phlegm?
[SEG0013] person_2 (PATIENT): No. No blood. I'd have panicked.
[SEG0014] person_3 (DOCTOR): Are you getting short of breath?
[SEG0015] person_2 (PATIENT): On the stairs, yes, a bit. On the flat I'm fine. We've got those steep cottage stairs, mind.
[SEG0016] person_3 (DOCTOR): Any chest pain?
[SEG0017] person_2 (PATIENT): No, none.
[SEG0018] person_3 (DOCTOR): Any fever at the moment, or sweats that soak the sheets?
[SEG0019] person_2 (PATIENT): I was proper feverish with the flu, burning up, but that's settled. No drenching sweats. I just get warm from coughing under the duvet.
[SEG0020] person_3 (DOCTOR): Have you lost any weight?
[SEG0021] person_2 (PATIENT): No, I don't think so. Appetite's all right. Linda's been bringing those beef stews round.
[SEG0022] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Which she pushes round the plate, if I'm honest.
[SEG0023] person_3 (DOCTOR): Have you travelled abroad recently, or been in contact with anyone with tuberculosis?
[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): No. No travel — garden centre is as far as I get these days. And no, nobody with TB.
[SEG0025] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Hang on, Janet. Cousin Martin was in with a bad chest and they were talking about TB. You went over with that fish pie.
[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): That was not TB, Linda. It was last year, and they never said it was definite. I didn't catch a thing.
[SEG0027] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): I can't swear to last year. Could've been this spring, I can't pin the month. But tuberculosis was mentioned — I heard it myself on the ward.

[SEG0028] person_3 (DOCTOR): So I'll note that you don't recall any recent travel or any definite TB contact, while Linda remembers a cousin who may have had tuberculosis, and neither of you can date that firmly. I'm not drawing a conclusion from it.

[SEG0029] person_2 (PATIENT): Oh, and while I think of it, you asked about weight. Well, actually, my trousers are loose and I've had to pull the belt in two holes. Past few weeks, I suppose — I didn't clock it as weight until just now.

[SEG0030] person_3 (DOCTOR): Thank you, that's useful. The cough has run six weeks since the flu, worse at night, mostly dry with a little clear phlegm in the morning, a bit breathless on the stairs, and your trousers have got loose over the past few weeks. No blood, no chest pain, no fever now, and no drenching sweats.
[SEG0031] person_3 (DOCTOR): Let me listen to your chest. Take a deep breath, and again. Your chest is clear, no crackles and no wheeze, and your throat looks unremarkable.
[SEG0032] person_2 (PATIENT): Well that's something. I was sure it'd sound like my old kettle rattling.
[SEG0033] person_3 (DOCTOR): What medicines do you take?

[SEG0034] person_2 (PATIENT): Amlodipine, five milligrams, once in the morning, for my blood pressure — years I've been on that. And at night I've been taking Covonia from the chemist, maybe two spoonfuls, I'm not certain of the amount. It takes the edge off, not much else.
[SEG0035] person_3 (DOCTOR): Any drug allergies?
[SEG0036] person_2 (PATIENT): No, nothing. Never had a problem with medicines.
[SEG0037] person_3 (DOCTOR): Do you smoke?
[SEG0038] person_2 (PATIENT): Never. I packed in the post office five years ago, so I'm not around the sorting-office dust anymore. I live on my own — Linda just tags along to these things.

[SEG0039] person_3 (DOCTOR): I'm turning a few things over: a cough that lingers after flu, some airway irritation, and your blood pressure tablet isn't usually the culprit the way an ACE inhibitor can be. I haven't forgotten what Linda said about your cousin, but I'm not going to name a cause today. What I will do is arrange a chest X-ray.
[SEG0040] person_2 (PATIENT): An X-ray, right. I had one years ago for my shoulder, not the chest. Will it show if something's lurking?

[SEG0041] person_3 (DOCTOR): It will show us the lungs properly, which is what we need before anyone guesses. I'll see you back here once the report is through, usually within a week. If you cough up blood, or you become much more breathless, ring the surgery the same day or go to A&E. Carry on the amlodipine as usual.
[SEG0042] person_1 (NURSE): I'll book that chest X-ray at the hospital before you go, Mrs Hale. Pop back to the corridor and I'll call you.
